name: IPR Enforcement Directive
evidence_rating: thin to moderate: one credible natural-experiment study (Sweden) plus Commission reviews that found no measurable effect on litigation
summary: The 2004 directive harmonised the court tools rights holders can use against IP infringers. A Swedish study found that when the rules came in, file-sharing fell and music sales rose sharply for some months before fading, with no effect on film sales. The Commission's 2017 evaluation judged the directive cheap and useful, but found no measurable effect on court enforcement across the EU, and counterfeiting kept rising.

indicators.objective: The 2003 proposal has no indicators section; Article 18 required a Commission report three years after transposition
Effective civil enforcement of IP rights
indicators.indicator: Harmonised measures: evidence, right of information, injunctions, damages, legal costs
indicators.evidence: 2010 report: 'substantial and positive effect'. 2017 evaluation: improved enforcement conceptually, but econometric models found no statistically measurable effect on litigation indicators; application diverges across courts.

Sweden's 2009 implementation cut internet traffic 18% and raised music sales (physical +27%, digital +48%) over six months, with no effect on films; effects faded later. Commission notes counterfeiting still rising EU-wide.
Evaluation study found no incremental direct costs from the Directive; average firm spends about EUR 115,000 a year on IP enforcement overall.

literature.citation: European Commission (2010), Report on the application of Directive 2004/48/EC on the enforcement of intellectual property rights (with SEC(2010) 1589), COM(2010) 779
literature.title: Report on the application of Directive 2004/48/EC on the enforcement of intellectual property rights (with SEC(2010) 1589)
literature.headline: Directive had a 'substantial and positive effect' on civil protection of IP rights, but was not designed for the challenge of internet infringements; issues with right of information, damages and intermediaries
literature.summary_plain: The first review found the directive had strengthened IP enforcement in court but was not built for online piracy.

literature.citation: European Commission (2017), Evaluation of Directive 2004/48/EC (accompanying guidance communication), SWD(2017) 431
literature.title: Evaluation of Directive 2004/48/EC (accompanying guidance communication)
literature.method: evaluation study incl. econometric analysis of IP court cases 2005-2015, consultation
literature.headline: Directive improved civil enforcement at a conceptual level and imposed no incremental direct costs; but econometric models found no strong correlation, let alone causality, between the Directive and litigation indicators; benefits cannot be quantified; counterfeiting and piracy still rising
literature.summary_plain: The 2017 evaluation judged the directive useful and cheap, but could find no measurable effect on court enforcement, and counterfeiting kept growing.

literature.citation: Adermon & Liang (2014), Piracy and music sales: The effects of an anti-piracy law, Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization 105
literature.title: Piracy and music sales: The effects of an anti-piracy law
literature.method: natural experiment (time-series around Sweden's IPRED implementation, 1 April 2009)
literature.headline: Working-paper version: reform cut Swedish internet traffic by 18% over six months and raised physical music sales 27% and digital 48%; no significant effect on cinema tickets or DVDs; press coverage of the published version reports smaller figures (traffic -16%, music sales +36%) and fading effects
literature.summary_plain: When Sweden implemented the directive, file-sharing dropped and music sales jumped for several months, but film sales did not change and the effect faded.
literature.quality: credible causal design; single country, short-run
